 LYNCHBURG, Va. (WSET) — More than 70 years after serving on the front lines of the Korean War, a Lynchburg veteran is still trying to make sure the lessons of that conflict aren't lost.
 Bevin Alexander was just 22 when he was called into service in 1950. An Army officer and recent Citadel graduate, he was assigned to a little-known military organization with an unusual mission: document the war as it happened.
 Army Lieutenant Bevin Alexander at the 3rd Infantry Division front west of Chorwon in February 1952. (Photo: Bevin Alexander) 
 Alexander became commander of the Army's 5th Historical Detachment, one of seven units created to monitor combat operations, record what was happening on the battlefield and report directly to the Pentagon.
 He arrived in Korea in June 1951 and went straight to the front.
 I was suddenly transported from being a civilian at a newspaper in North Carolina to Korea in the space of about 10 days," Alexander recalled. His job on the battlefield put him in places most Americans would never see.
 He traveled by Army jeep, carried his own cot, typewriter and notebooks, and followed military operations wherever he believed he needed to be.
 His orders allowed him to go to "points deemed necessary" throughout Korea.
 Among the battles he documented was Bloody Ridge, one of the bloodiest engagements of the Korean War.
 I reported the very first shots that were being fired against the place which became the quintessential battle of the Korean War called Bloody Ridge," he said. Alexander and the other historical detachment officers weren't simply recording individual accounts. Their studies would become a foundation for the historical record of the war.
 Army Lieutenant Bevin Alexander on the troopship in Sasebo harbor, Kyushu Island, Japan, as he departed for San Francisco and home in August 1952. (Photo: Bevin Alexander) 
 Looking back, he said the responsibility weighed heavily on him. He was the youngest of the officers commanding the historical detachments, many of whom were college history professors.
 But while Alexander was documenting the fighting, the American public was hearing remarkably little about it.
 He believes there was a deliberate reason.
 Alexander says the U.S. government intentionally downplayed the Korean War in the public eye because leaders feared it could expand into another world war.
 By 1951, the Soviet Union also had an atomic bomb. Alexander said the danger of a broader conflict and the possibility of an atomic war shaped how the administration wanted the Korean War presented to the American public.
 "The basic thing we were trying to do in Korea was to keep the war in Korea and not extend it to a world war," Alexander said.
 He explained that the government wanted military information documented and sent to the Pentagon, but did not want the public to become increasingly focused on the conflict or demand a wider confrontation with China and Russia.
 That distinction, he believes, helps explain why so many Americans knew so little about the fighting.
 Alexander said newspapers ultimately helped cement the name "Forgotten War": a war that claimed the lives of 36,574 Americans and wounded 103,284. More than 7,400 remain unaccounted for. 
 He recalled one major newspaper publishing the same Korean War story for five consecutive days without changing it and receiving no public reaction.
 "Because the ordinary public didn't know anything about the war," he said.
 For those serving in Korea, the lack of attention followed them home.
 Alexander remembers returning to the United States and finding that few people even knew where he had been.
 I remember when I came home that nobody had paid any attention to the fact that I was a veteran of the Korean War," he said. Alexander's experience eventually became the foundation for his book, "Korea: The First War We Lost."
 At the urging of his son, Bevin Alexander wrote this book, Korea: The First War We Lost. In the international bestseller, Alexander argued that the United States failed to achieve victory because political and military leaders repeatedly abandoned indirect, maneuvering strategies in favor of a costly, head-on war of attrition against communist forces. (Photo: Bevin Alexander) 
 His son, Bevin Alexander Jr., who lives in Lynchburg, encouraged his father to write about what he had witnessed firsthand. The book became an international bestseller and was later translated into Chinese.
 His father's firsthand experience gave the book a perspective that couldn't be replicated by someone studying the war from a distance, his son said.
 Alexander went on to write 16 books. But his interest in history has always extended beyond documenting what happened. He wants people to understand what history should teach us.
 And he isn't convinced we've been listening.
 ABC13's Pat Simon asked Alexander whether the country has learned from its experiences in Korea, Vietnam and Afghanistan. Alexander said he doesn't believe we have.
 He pointed to the difficulty of using military force to make another country adopt a desired outcome, arguing that the resistance of the people being fought cannot simply be overcome.
 "The fact is that we really do not learn from history, I don't think," he said. "And I think this is the perfect example of it."
 Now 98, Alexander lives at Bentley Commons Senior Living in Lynchburg. Glaucoma has taken his eyesight, leaving him unable to read the books and historical accounts that defined much of his life.
 Bevin Alexander, author of 13 books on military history, served as a combat historian during the Korean War. (Photo: Bevin Alexander) 
 "I wish I could read. I can't read anymore," he said. "That's a great pain to me because that's what I've basically done all my life."
 His son now helps him revisit the past.
 For Alexander, the men who served in Korea deserve to be remembered not simply for the battles they fought, but for the sense of duty that carried them there.
 His son believes those sacrifices should never be forgotten.
 These men all felt a sense of duty that they owed the nation," Bevin Alexander Jr. said. "They should be remembered for that because they made big sacrifices." This Veterans Day, Alexander's story is a reminder that honoring veterans means more than thanking them for their service. It also means listening to what they witnessed and considering what their experiences can teach the generations that follow.
